record.paper_title: Quantum Communication: From Fundamentals to Recent Trends, Challenges and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can quantum error correction for quantum computation and quantum communication protect quantum information against noise, decoherence, leakage, measurement errors, bit-flip errors, phase errors, and continuous-angle errors while respecting the no-cloning constraint that prevents simply storing duplicate copies of qubits?

evidence.quote: the goal of Quantum Error Correction (QEC) [149] [150] is to detect and correct errors that occur during quantum computations or quantum communication. It involves encoding quantum information into quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) [151] [152] [153] [154] to protect against errors caused by noise, decoherence, and other sources of interference.

Although the basic principles for quantum error correction are the same as in classical error correction schemes, there are certain challenges that need to be addressed for implementing QEC as follows. 1. Unlike classical counterpart, quantum errors cannot be resolved by storing a duplicate copy of the quantum states or qubits. This is because of the ‘No cloning Theorem’. 2. Quantum errors include both bits-flip errors and phase errors. To generalize, quantum errors are continuous in nature, that is, there are errors that can result in shift of quantum bits by an angle.
Other kinds of quantum errors include qubit leakage [155] [156] [157] and measurement errors.

artifact.status_search_result: Foundational results (Shor code, stabilizer formalism, CSS codes, Knill–Laflamme conditions, and the threshold theorem for fault-tolerant quantum computation) demonstrate that discrete Pauli errors, continuous rotations (via discretization), and many decoherence models can be corrected, and leakage-reduction units and measurement-error mitigation techniques exist. Recent experimental demonstrations (e.g., surface code below threshold on Google's Willow processor in 2024–2025) confirm partial practical progress. However, a fully unified, optimal scheme that simultaneously handles all listed error types with provable thresholds in realistic hardware remains an active research area, so the broad question is partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Quantum Error Correction and Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
status_evidence.snippet: The threshold theorem shows that arbitrary-length quantum computation is possible if physical error rates are below a constant threshold, addressing discrete and (via discretization) continuous errors.
status_evidence.claim: Threshold theorem partially resolves protection against generic noise, but unified handling of all error types remains active.

status_evidence.title: Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold (Google Quantum AI, 2024)
status_evidence.snippet: Demonstration of surface-code logical qubits with error rates suppressed below threshold as code distance increases.
status_evidence.claim: Experimental progress shows partial solution of the practical QEC problem.

status_evidence.title: Leakage reduction units
status_evidence.snippet: Schemes to convert leakage errors into standard Pauli errors that stabilizer codes can correct.
status_evidence.claim: Leakage component has dedicated partial solutions.
